[verifier] The int sum of 0..99,999,999 overflows a signed int (undefined behaviour), and because the results are unused an optimised build may delete the array test entirely (new/delete pairs may be elided since C++14), so a 650 ms array time with a several-second push_back vector fits an unoptimised build better than a release one. In Qt 6, QVector<int> is an alias of QList<int>.

corrections.workload: Chapter06/03_owning_ptr_mbm.C against 03b_shared_ptr_mbm.C and 03a_raw_ptr_mbm.C (Google Benchmark, ThreadRange(1, numcpu) so 1, 2, 4, ... threads all running the same operation, real time): BM_ptr_deref copies the published object through the pointer and BM_ptr_assign publishes a pointer, 64 unrolled operations per iteration; there is no mixed reader/writer run. ts_unique_ptr is a std::atomic<T*> with release publish and acquire get.
corrections.caveats: The timing numbers are the book's own (quoted in the seed lead); the repository carries the benchmark program but no results file, so the numbers do not appear on the benchmark_url page and the ratios could not be checked against it. The 60x is mostly the cost of the library's atomic shared_ptr access: libstdc++ and libc++ have implemented std::atomic_load on a shared_ptr through a global mutex pool, so the ratio depends on the standard library and version (C++20 std::atomic<std::shared_ptr> differs again) and the book does not name it. Compiler, flags and CPU not stated. The baseline does extra work (reference counting) that the publishing pointer avoids by design, so it is a different safety contract and not a like-for-like swap. [verifier] Harness defects: REPEAT expands to 64 operations per iteration in all three files but SetItemsProcessed counts 32, so items-per-second figures (and any per-operation time derived from them) are off by a factor of 2; the ratios between files are unaffected because all share the error. ts_unique_ptr's operator= publishes without deleting the previous object (the delete is commented out), so the publishing pointer leaks on reassignment and offers no reclamation, which is the work the shared_ptr baseline pays for: each 03b dereference copies a shared_ptr through atomic_load_explicit (a lock from the mutex pool plus a reference-count increment and decrement). The raw-pointer file calls ClobberMemory every iteration while the owning-pointer file does not. The Chapter06 listing has no std::unique_ptr benchmark, so the 'matches std::unique_ptr' part of the claim is the book's text only.
